messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq is a 56-year-old married man of Lebanese descent who works as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing firm. He presented for intake reporting a PCL-5 score of 48, following an incident of police violence that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. He had been attending a community vigil in his neighborhood when officers moved in to disperse the crowd. In the chaos that followed, Tariq was shoved to the ground, struck repeatedly, and held face-down on the pavement with his arm wrenched behind his back. He recalls the specific, acrid taste of blood and asphalt in his mouth as his face was pressed against the ground — a detail that returns to him unbidden and with nauseating fidelity. He remembers screaming that he had done nothing wrong, and that no one intervened. It is this last fact — the bystanders, the silence, the faces that looked away — that has since become the organizing wound of his inner life.

In the weeks that followed, Tariq found that the world had rearranged itself around a single conviction: that people are not what they seem, that those who appear neutral or friendly are capable of indifference or complicity at the moment it matters most. He had also come to believe, with a shame he could not fully articulate, that he had acted in ways that went against who he was — that he had begged, that he had not fought back, that something essential had been surrendered on that pavement. These appraisals — that the world is dangerous, that others cannot be trusted, that he had violated his own values — did not remain abstract. They drove him toward a set of strategies that, over months, quietly restructured his life. He began avoiding anything that might stir feeling: he stopped watching television, refused to read news, and withdrew from the cultural commentary that had once been the lifeblood of his professional enthusiasm. He had come to believe that if he could keep his emotional register flat, he could remain safe.

But the sense of safety never came. At work, where his job requires him to monitor and curate social media feeds, Tariq finds himself scanning not just for relevant content but for anything that might signal threat — a raised voice in the open-plan office, a colleague approaching from behind, the flash of a police uniform in a video thumbnail. Before he attends any meeting, he identifies the exits. He cannot sit with his back to the door. He has told his wife he simply prefers certain seats at restaurants; she has not yet understood that he is mapping escape routes. This persistent state of threat monitoring — the inability to relax even in spaces he knows to be objectively safe — feeds back directly into his worst appraisals. The fact that he cannot feel safe anywhere confirms, in his private reasoning, that the world truly is dangerous and that his distrust of others is simply realism rather than symptom.

The memories themselves have become a site of active struggle. When the recall surfaces — triggered most often by the taste of something metallic, or by video footage of crowds on his work screen — it arrives with an intensity of rage that frightens him. He has learned to push the memory away before it can fully form, cutting it off before it reaches its conclusion. Yet this suppression, which offers momentary relief, appears to be sustaining the very threat state it was meant to quiet: the incomplete, repeatedly interrupted memory leaves him in a state of unresolved physiological arousal that makes relaxation impossible and keeps his scanning behavior constant. The avoidance, in turn, forecloses the kind of emotional processing that might soften his appraisals; because he never allows himself to feel through the event, his beliefs about his own violated character and the world's fundamental danger remain untested and intact. The loop has grown tighter over fourteen months. He is, by his own account, exhausted.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a moment at work last month when he deleted an entire week's worth of scheduled content — posts he himself had written — because a single image reminded him of the vigil. His supervisor noticed. Tariq is most afraid that he will never trust another person again. What he hopes for, quietly, is to be able to sit in a room and simply not be waiting for something terrible to happen.
